issues.description: The problem statement asks students to implement a function named _detect_errors(...) (leading underscore) but the template and reference solution provide/expect a function named detect_errors(...) (no underscore). This name mismatch between the specification and the provided code will confuse students about which function to implement and may cause tests to fail or be unclear about the intended entry point.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the function name consistent across all artifacts. Either (A) update the problem statement to refer to detect_errors(...) (no underscore), or (B) add a thin wrapper in the template named _detect_errors that calls detect_errors so both names are accepted. Ensure tests and any examples use the same name.

issues.description: The problem statement asks students to implement a function named `_detect_errors(...)`, while both the template code and the reference solution use the name `detect_errors(...)` (no leading underscore). This inconsistent identifier for the same conceptual entity (the routine that checks measurement outcomes against parity checks) can confuse students about which function to implement and which name the tests expect.
issues.suggestedFix: Use a single consistent name for the error-detection function across all artifacts. Update the problem statement to refer to `detect_errors(...)` (remove the leading underscore), or alternatively change the template and solution to provide/alias `_detect_errors(...)`, so students and tests see the same identifier.
